parts.move: state how a gradient's units are derived from the axes
parts.prompt: State how to find the units of a graph's gradient from the units of the two axes, and give an example.
scheme: Gradient units = (y-axis unit) ÷ (x-axis unit)
Example: gradient of velocity–time has units m s⁻¹ ÷ s = m s⁻²
parts.answer: A gradient divides the y-quantity by the x-quantity, so its units divide likewise: velocity over time gives m s⁻¹ per s = m s⁻² — the acceleration. Units you cannot name from the axes mean the axes are mislabelled.

parts.move: state the general strategy for linearising a power-law relationship
parts.prompt: You believe y = kaⁿ relates two measured quantities. State what to plot to test this as a straight line, and what the gradient and intercept give.
scheme: Take logs: log y = n log a + log k
Plot log y against log a
Gradient = n (the power), intercept = log k
A straight line confirms the power law; curvature rejects it
parts.answer: Linearise by taking logarithms: log y = n·log a + log k. Plot log y against log a — a straight line proves the power law, with gradient reading off the exponent n and intercept giving log k. Lines are easier to judge than curves, which is why physicists log things.

parts.move: explain how the worst acceptable line yields a gradient uncertainty
parts.prompt: Explain how you would obtain an uncertainty in the gradient of a best-fit line using error bars, and how the gradient's percentage uncertainty feeds into a derived quantity.
scheme: Draw the steepest and shallowest straight lines still consistent with the error bars
Worst-line gradient difference from the best-fit gradient gives the absolute uncertainty (often half the spread)
Percentage gradient uncertainty = Δgrad/grad × 100
If the quantity equals the gradient directly, that percentage carries straight through; if divided by another measurement, the percentages add
parts.answer: The best-fit line's slope is not a fact but an estimate bounded by the data's error bars: the steepest and shallowest lines that still thread the bars give extreme gradients whose half-spread estimates the uncertainty. If the constant you want IS the gradient, its percentage error simply passes on; if you then divide by another reading, percentages combine — the line is uncertainty, graphed.

parts.move: explain how a non-zero intercept exposes a systematic error or unmodelled term
parts.prompt: A resistance–length graph for a wire has gradient ρ/A but cuts the resistance axis at +0.4 Ω instead of the origin. Explain what that intercept likely represents, and why forcing the line through zero would be wrong.
scheme: The 0.4 Ω offset is extra series resistance: leads, contacts or ammeter resistance the model ignored
It behaves as a constant added to every reading — a systematic offset
Forcing zero would bias the gradient as well: the fit must let physics put the offset where the data say
parts.answer: The wire itself contributes ρL/A — zero at zero length — so the surviving 0.4 Ω must come from elsewhere: crocodile clips, lead resistance, or the ammeter's own resistance. The intercept is the experiment telling you about the unmodelled series resistance. Pinning the line to zero doesn't remove that resistance; it only hides the clue and bends the gradient to cover it up.

parts.move: choose the axes that linearise a stated proposed relationship
parts.prompt: A student expects the extension x of a rubber band to grow with the hanging mass m as x = b·m^c. State the plot that turns this into a straight line and what c and log b are read from.
scheme: log x = c·log m + log b
Plot log x (y-axis) against log m (x-axis)
Gradient gives c; intercept gives log b
Curvature in this plot would reject the power-law form
parts.answer: Take logs of x = b·m^c: log x = c log m + log b. Log-extension against log-mass must then be straight, its gradient the exponent c and its intercept log b. If the logged points still curve, the power-law assumption is dead — which the original x-m graph could only hint at.

parts.move: compute a gradient using a large triangle on the line of best fit
parts.prompt: On a T² (s²) against L (m) graph for a pendulum, the best-fit line passes through (0.30 m, 1.21 s²) and (1.00 m, 4.04 s²). Calculate the gradient and the implied g. (T² = 4π²L/g)
scheme: Use the line's points, not raw data points off the line
parts.answer: The long triangle across the line gives 4.04 s² m⁻¹. With T² = (4π²/g)L, g = 4π²/gradient = 9.77 m s⁻². The arithmetic is nothing special — the method is: measure the gradient of the line, never of two scattered points, because the line has already averaged every reading.

parts.move: reject connecting points (or forcing through all) instead of a best-fit line
parts.prompt: A student draws a curve through every plotted point and says it is more accurate because it touches all the data. Explain why that misrepresents the results.
scheme: Every point carries measurement scatter; a curve through all of them bakes noise into the model
A best-fit line averages the scatter — it represents the mean trend, not each reading
Accuracy is improved by the fit's averaging, not by preserving each individual error
parts.answer: The points' individual errors are the very thing the graph should average away; a line kissing every dot memorises the mistakes instead. The best-fit line's distance from the points IS the scatter — discarding it doesn't add accuracy, it hides the measurement quality. The line should have the dots around it, none of them on command.

parts.move: read a power-law exponent from logged data values
parts.prompt: log₁₀(T/s) rises by 0.50 while log₁₀(L/m) rises by 1.00 for a pendulum's data. State the exponent relating T to L and write the resulting proportional law.
scheme: Gradient = 0.50/1.00 = 0.5 = the power n
So T ∝ L^0.5 = √L
Equivalent: T² ∝ L — the familiar pendulum relation
parts.answer: A gradient of 0.5 in log-log space means T ∝ L^½ — the square-root law, equivalently T² ∝ L. The logged rise-ratio did in two numbers what the pendulum's whole theory says in one: period grows with the root of length.

parts.move: transfer linearisation to a reciprocal rearrangement extracting two constants from one line
parts.prompt: A battery of unknown emf ε and internal resistance r drives currents I through variable resistors R, so ε = I(R + r). State what to plot to get a straight line from which both ε and r can be found, and identify the gradient and intercept.
scheme: Rearrange: R = ε(1/I) − r
Plot R (y-axis) against 1/I (x-axis)
Gradient = ε; intercept on the R-axis = −r
Alternatively plot 1/I against R: gradient = 1/ε, intercept = r/ε
parts.answer: Rearrange ε = I(R+r) to R = ε/I − r: plotting R against 1/I gives a straight line whose gradient is the emf and whose negative intercept is the internal resistance. One rearrangement hands two hidden constants to two obvious features of a single line.

parts.move: combine gradient-based resistivity extraction with uncertainty propagation to report a material constant
parts.prompt: A wire's resistance-vs-length graph has gradient 2.2 ± 0.2 Ω m⁻¹; its diameter is measured as 0.30 ± 0.01 mm. Calculate the resistivity and its percentage uncertainty, and state which measurement should be improved first. (Give 2 s.f.)
scheme: Gradient percentage = 0.2/2.2 ≈ 9%; diameter's 3% doubles through the square → 6%
Total ≈ 15% — the gradient (graph) dominates, improve the fit data first
parts.answer: ρ = (R/L)×A = 2.2×7.07×10⁻⁸ ≈ 1.6×10⁻⁷ Ω m — nichrome territory. Uncertainties: the gradient contributes 9%; the diameter's 3% becomes 6% squared. At ~15% combined, the graph's scatter is the villain, so the next round means more length readings and tighter contacts — a micrometer can only fix a smaller slice.

parts.move: combine exponential decay with linearisation to extract the decay constant from a log graph
parts.prompt: Count-rate data for a source is linearised as ln(A/s⁻¹) against t/s, giving a straight line of gradient −0.035 s⁻¹ and intercept 7.0. Calculate the decay constant and the initial activity.
scheme: A = A₀e^(−λt) → ln A = −λt + ln A₀
Gradient = −λ → λ = 0.035 s⁻¹
Intercept ln A₀ = 7.0 → A₀ = e⁷·⁰ ≈ 1.1×10³ s⁻¹
Half-life check: t½ = ln2/λ ≈ 20 s
parts.answer: The logged straight line has gradient −λ, so λ = 0.035 s⁻¹ (t½ = 0.693/0.035 ≈ 20 s), and the intercept e⁷·⁰ gives an initial activity near 1100 s⁻¹. An exponential decay is a straight line wearing logarithmic make-up — the graph reads both the rate and the start from one ruler.
